title: Will the Opportunity Corridor Live Up to its Name?
abstract: The Opportunity Corridor is a 5-lane boulevard running from an interchange with I-490 and I-77 in the southwest to University Circle and the Cleveland Clinic’s main campus in the northeast. Initially conceived as a limited-access freeway running through Cleveland’s eastern inner core, the road was built as a full-access urban boulevard with a stated purpose of "improving the roadway network within a historically underserved, economically depressed area" and "improving system linkage, improving mobility and supporting planned economic development". Construction began in 2013, and the road was fully completed in 2021 at a total cost of $330 million. The Corridor’s completion has stirred mixed reactions: supporters highlight reduced travel times and business growth along its route, while critics question its economic impact, arguing that the road primarily serves to improve highway access for affluent employees and residents of University Circle.
paragraph1: Cleveland’s "Opportunity Corridor" is a 5-lane boulevard running from an interchange with I-490 and I-77 in the southwest to University Circle and the Cleveland Clinic’s main campus in the northeast. Initially conceived as a limited-access freeway running through Cleveland’s eastern inner core, the road was built as a full-access urban boulevard with a stated purpose of "improving the roadway network within a historically underserved, economically depressed area" and "improving system linkage, improving mobility and supporting planned economic development" (will create citation). Construction began in 2013, and the road was fully completed in 2021 at a total cost of $330 million.
paragraph2: The Corridor’s completion has stirred mixed reactions: supporters highlight reduced travel times and business growth along its route, while critics question its economic impact, arguing that the road primarily serves to improve highway access for affluent employees and residents of University Circle (link1, link2).
paragraph3: The Opportunity Corridor runs through some of Cleveland’s most economically depressed areas. According to American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, in the five years prior to the completion of the first stage of the Corridor, census tracts adjacent to the Corridor’s route had among the lowest median household incomes and highest unemployment rates in all of Cleveland and Cuyahoga County. Typical household incomes were around $20,000, below the 2015 poverty level for a 4-person household, and unemployment exceeded 30% in some tracts. According to ACS data, residents in a selection of 12 tracts along the corridor were twice as likely to take public transportation to work and less likely to hold a high school diploma or a degree of higher education compared to those in the rest of Cuyahoga County and the nation as a whole.
paragraph4: Home values reflect the area’s poor economic state and show its decline over time relative to the rest of Cleveland. In 2007, home values between Cleveland’s eastern and western core were comparable. Hough, a neighborhood a few miles east of downtown, had among the highest home values in Cleveland. By 2014, the Great Recession had pushed home values down significantly across the city, but there remained relative parity between the east and west sides. In the years that followed, home values recovered much faster in western suburbs, while values in the city’s eastern inner core stagnated. Now, neighborhoods adjacent to the opportunity corridor, such as Kinsman, Woodland Hills, and Fairfax, have home values much lower than most west-side neighborhoods. University Circle, home to Case Western Reserve University and Little Italy, is an exception.
paragraph5: This chart depicts the uneven intracity recovery from the Great Recession. Pre-Great Recession, Fairfax, Kinsman, and Woodland Hills had home values in the top half of all Cleveland neighborhoods. Now, these neighborhoods are in the bottom 25%. There does not appear to be any bump in home values in these neighborhoods from the Corridor’s construction start in 2013, first-stage completion in 2018, and final completion in 2021.
paragraph6: Now that the Corridor has been open for several years, have economic circumstances in the area changed? Anecdotally, there is evidence of some business growth along the Corridor. In early October 2024, Nor-Am Cold Storage opened a $50 million, 160,000-square-foot cold storage facility on the corner of Opportunity Corridor and East 75th Street (link). Across the street, Orlando Baking Company is actively hiring, and CEO John Orlando reports that delivery times have been trimmed and it’s easier for his employees to get to work. Farm House Foods and Miceli Dairy Products, businesses located along the corridor, also report improved efficiency and easier commutes for employees (link). Still, much of the Corridor is lined with empty lots, waiting for development that has yet to come.
paragraph7: For those living near the corridor, there doesn’t appear to be any evidence that circumstances have improved. Comparing 5-year ACS estimates from before and after the Corridor’s first-stage completion for selected tracts adjacent to the Corridor shows the unemployment rate has risen relative to the rest of Cuyahoga County and the nation. At the same time, the labor force participation rate has fallen significantly. Between these two periods, the population in these tracts has also fallen by over half,from an average of 107,000 from 2013-2017 to just 51,000 from 2018-2022. This mass exodus could explain the declining workforce participation rate if those leaving tended to be younger and of working age. Finally, with a new road intended to reduce travel times, one might expect commute times to decrease; instead, the proportion of workers with long commutes of over 30 minutes increased significantly, while falling in the rest of Cuyahoga County. Alternatively, this could suggest that the Corridor has had a positive effect on job access, as residents could be commuting farther to new jobs that previously would have been unreasonably long commutes.
paragraph8: For the most part, it appears the Opportunity Corridor has yet to deliver on its goal of increased economic activity in areas adjacent to its route. While the project has created potential for new industrial sites, many of these remain empty several years after the road’s completion. As Jeff Epstein, Cleveland's chief of integrated development, noted, “The Opportunity Corridor has 10-plus acre sites that can be assembled if a company wants to come in. There’s a lack of these in the city” (Williams & Chilcote, 2023). This availability of large sites could attract industries like food production, health care, and advanced manufacturing, with a focus on creating jobs. According to Epstein, the city's vision includes clustering healthcare and tech jobs near University Circle and positioning food production and manufacturing elsewhere along the corridor. Yet, even with these prospects, the question remains: Where is the opportunity? While the road is in place, areas adjacent to the Corridor are yet to see any significant improvements, revealing a gap between the project's goals and the current reality for the people who live nearby. The potential consequences of this unfulfilled promise are significant. Without the anticipated job creation and community investment, residents may face continued economic stagnation, and continuing cycles of poverty.
paragraph9: Mike Kash, whose business, Kash Auto Parts & Salvage, lost property due to the development. “We’ve been in this location for the last 40 years,” (Shookman, 2021) Kash remarked, reflecting on the toll that the project has taken on his livelihood.
